processes.description: Bill Williams III explains to the desk how decremental and tiered adjustment bids are placed in the CAISO market and run on behalf of generators. Each round is one explanatory message: he asks what tools were used to settle earlier bids, attaches a simple sheet outlining the basic decremental bidding process, says the desk will work with generators on buy-backs or supplemental dec bids when market conditions warrant, sets the tiering process as the way forward, and warns of the CAISO cap on how many tiered bids its system reads.
steps: Find out which tools were used to settle earlier decremental bids.
Write up the basic decremental bidding process on a simple sheet and send it to the desk.
Work with the generators on buy-backs or supplemental dec bids when market conditions warrant.
Tier the adjustment bids using the process the desk has developed.
Keep each tiered bid set within the number of bids the CAISO system will read.

stalls.summary: The CAISO system stops reading tiered adjustment bids past its cap, so bid sets have to be cut down to fit and the desk has to be warned about the limit.
How earlier decremental bids were settled is not written down; the author has to ask colleagues which settlement tools were used.

automation.approach: A bid-building sheet that lays out decremental and tiered adjustment bids per generator, checks the tier count against the CAISO read limit before submission, and records which settlement tool applies, paired with a written procedure for dec bidding and generator buy-backs.
automation.rationale: The mail is one trader explaining the same bidding method to the desk in pieces: the process sheet, the tiering rule, the generator buy-backs and the system cap. A single written procedure captures that knowledge once and answers the settlement-tool question the mail had to ask.

processes.description: Volume management and accounting staff pass preliminary ledgers and inventory schedules round for review and settle the volumes that must be written off. A round starts with a file or a request: a ledger re-sent because the first copy was distorted, a request to move volumes determined to be written off at a meter, storage inventory schedules put together for Spindletop and Bammel, or a request to help resolve differences between figures. Recipients research the volumes, reconcile the differences and process the write-off, with forwards and chasers when answers are slow.
steps: Send the preliminary ledger or inventory schedule to the reviewers.
Re-send the file if the first copy arrives unreadable.
Research the meter volumes flagged to be written off.
Put together the inventory schedules for the storage facilities such as Spindletop and Bammel.
Ask the logistics and accounting contacts to help resolve the differences found.
Book the agreed volume or general ledger write-off.

stalls.summary: The first copy of the ledger file arrived distorted and had to be sent again before anyone could review it.
Differences between the figures stay open until several people are asked to help resolve them, and write-off volumes at a meter wait on someone to move them to the right place.

automation.approach: A standard reconciliation report that pulls scheduled, measured and booked volumes by meter and storage facility, flags differences above a tolerance, and pre-fills the write-off entry and the Spindletop and Bammel inventory schedules, leaving staff to research the flagged items and approve the write-off.
automation.rationale: The repetitive work is assembling schedules and lining up volumes from different sources so differences show. A fixed schedule and reconciliation layout makes the differences visible in one place and cuts the rework of re-sent or distorted files, while the decision to write off stays with people.

work_estimate.rationale: Time goes to research rather than mail: tracing the meter volumes to be written off, building the Spindletop and Bammel inventory schedules, and working through the differences raised for resolution. A typical round of schedule building or volume research is put at 60 minutes; a simple re-sent ledger review near 30 minutes, a multi-facility schedule or a long reconciliation up to 150 minutes. Pulling volumes and laying out schedules can be generated by a report; researching causes and approving write-offs stays manual.

processes.description: Darron Giron supplies and chases the supporting detail behind monthly liquidation values. A round starts when support is needed for a month's liquidation values, such as the December liquidation values; he forwards the request to the person holding the detail, asks when the support may be available, and sends on a file with the volumes for the liquidations to the risk and accounting contacts.
steps: Receive or raise a request for support behind the month's liquidation values.
Forward the request to the contact who holds the supporting detail.
Ask when the support may be available.
Send the file with the liquidation volumes to the risk and accounting contacts.

stalls.summary: The support is not ready when asked for; the request goes out with a plea to be told when it may be available, so the round waits on the other party.

automation.approach: A standard liquidation support file produced each month from the deal and volume system, listing the volumes behind each liquidation value in a fixed layout, sent with the liquidation values so the risk and accounting contacts do not have to request it.
automation.rationale: Each round asks for the same thing: the volume detail behind the liquidation values. A fixed file layout that is filled and sent routinely removes the request and the wait shown in the mail.
